slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 22: Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

question.prompt: What is the central teaching rule for Modern C++?
question.answer: Do not praise an abstraction until you can explain the rule it encodes and the evidence that proves it behaves correctly.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

question.prompt: Why is “it compiled” not enough evidence?
question.answer: Compilation proves the source met translation rules, but it does not prove the intended runtime behavior, output contract, state invariant, or test case.

slides.title: Start with the failed contract
keyPoints: A useful diagnosis begins with an observable discrepancy.
“The application crashes” is a starting symptom.
“The second render reads a title after its parsing buffer has been reused” identifies a lifetime hypothesis.
“The destination changes after a rejected copy” identifies a state-guarantee discrepancy.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 22, treat Start with the failed contract as a design decision with costs and evidence. A useful diagnosis begins with an observable discrepancy. “The application crashes” is a starting symptom. “The second render reads a title after its parsing buffer has been reused” identifies a lifetime hypothesis. “The destination changes after a rejected copy” identifies a state-guarantee discrepancy. “Two equal-priority records change order” identifies a presentation contract. State the discrepancy before changing implementation details. Preserve the smallest reproducing input, the exact executable, compiler and library versions, build flags, arguments, working directory, exit status, and relevant output. Rebuilding the program before saving the failing binary can remove evidence. Reproducing with a new compiler can be useful, but it is a second experiment rather than a substitute for identifying what ran originally. The Linux book’s evidence-first habit applies directly to native application debugging. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

At translation time, inspect the first relevant diagnostic rather than the longest cascade. Confirm the selected language mode and that all required headers are included directly. A header that happens to arrive through another header on one implementation is not a dependable interface. When a concept fails, identify the expression or requirement that was not satisfied before weakening the constraint. Separate “the requested syntax is unavailable” from “the requested operation violates the template’s domain.” A C++20 build should not be repaired by assuming a C++23 library helper exists. A checked integer function rejecting bool should not be repaired by removing its concept. One failure concerns environment capability; the other concerns an intentional API boundary. slides.title: Gate 2 — Linking and target composition
keyPoints: A declaration tells translation what an entity looks like.
An out-of-line definition must also participate in the linked program when required.
If the report’s implementation file is absent from the target, repeatedly including its header will not resolve.
Inspect the CMake target and the actual build command, not only the editor’s file tree.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 22, treat Gate 2 — Linking and target composition as a design decision with costs and evidence. A declaration tells translation what an entity looks like. An out-of-line definition must also participate in the linked program when required. If the report’s implementation file is absent from the target, repeatedly including its header will not resolve the missing definition. Inspect the CMake target and the actual build command, not only the editor’s file tree. Templates have additional visibility requirements because needed instantiations often require definitions to be available where used. Moving every template body to a source file without an explicit instantiation design can produce linking failures. Decide whether the template is header-defined or explicitly instantiated for a closed set of types. Both are designs; an accidental mixture is not. slides.title: Gate 3 — Ownership and lifetime
keyPoints: For each suspect object, ask who constructed it, who destroys it, who can replace its storage, and which aliases.

The absence of the * character does not imply the absence of a borrow.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 22, treat Gate 3 — Ownership and lifetime as a design decision with costs and evidence. For each suspect object, ask who constructed it, who destroys it, who can replace its storage, and which aliases escaped. Trace raw pointers, references, iterators, spans, string views, lambda captures, and references embedded inside tuples. The absence of the * character does not imply the absence of a borrow. A pointer can be non-null and still be unusable. An iterator can have a plausible address and still be invalidated. A shared pointer can retain a control block while exposing an aliased subobject under a separate lifetime relationship. A const reference can prevent mutation through one name while another alias changes the owner. Diagnose the entire relationship, not a single reassuring property. slides.title: Gate 4 — Invariants and failure guarantees
keyPoints: Write the invariant as a statement that can be evaluated before and after the operation.
A buffer’s size must agree with its owned storage.
A report’s accepted IDs must be unique.
A quantity must stay within its domain.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 22, treat Gate 4 — Invariants and failure guarantees as a design decision with costs and evidence. Write the invariant as a statement that can be evaluated before and after the operation. A buffer’s size must agree with its owned storage. A report’s accepted IDs must be unique. A quantity must stay within its domain. A moved-from custom owner may promise an empty state. These statements identify what a test should inspect beyond the immediate return value. A basic exception guarantee preserves validity and avoids leaks under the operation’s contract. A strong guarantee preserves the specified observable state on failure. A nonthrowing operation promises that no exception escapes. These guarantees are not interchangeable, and each needs an explicit boundary. An operation can preserve a report while consuming input or changing a test fault counter. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Gate 5 — Algorithms and representation
keyPoints: Write the input domain, range category, comparator requirements, destination extent, mutation effects, and result.
A lower bound is not a membership result.
Stable sorting does not make output independent of input order.
Reserved vector capacity does not create destination elements.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 22, treat Gate 5 — Algorithms and representation as a design decision with costs and evidence. Write the input domain, range category, comparator requirements, destination extent, mutation effects, and result semantics. A lower bound is not a membership result. Stable sorting does not make output independent of input order. Reserved vector capacity does not create destination elements. A wider receiving variable does not widen an earlier narrow multiplication. For a container change, include how positions are found and which references are retained. A list’s insertion cost near a known iterator does not include a search for that iterator. A hash table’s average lookup behavior does not supply deterministic traversal order. A view’s concise syntax does not supply independent element ownership or cached computation. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.title: Gate 6 — External completion and evidence
keyPoints: Distinguish successful computation from successful publication.
A completed report string can exist while writing to its destination fails.
A successful file close is not a universal crash-durability guarantee.
A prior path inspection is not a held file handle.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 22, treat Gate 6 — External completion and evidence as a design decision with costs and evidence. Distinguish successful computation from successful publication. A completed report string can exist while writing to its destination fails. A successful file close is not a universal crash-durability guarantee. A prior path inspection is not a held file handle. A nonzero application exit can be the correct result of an expected rejection test. When reporting verification, name the actual configurations and cases executed. GCC and Clang may share the same standard library on a host. Sanitizers detect classes of defects in exercised executions; they do not prove semantic correctness or every path. Keep performance measurements separate from instrumented correctness runs, and do not publish a speedup without the baseline and workload that produced it. Use one short record per investigated change: the requirement; the smallest failing case; the relevant owner and invariant; the proposed mechanism; the expected failure boundary; the observed result; and the remaining limitation.
